title: OTP expiry
sources: Redis docs, EXPIRE: 'After the timeout has expired, the key will automatically be deleted' (the code 'disappears' on time to live).

RFC 6238 (TOTP): default time step 30 seconds; TOTP = HOTP(K, T) from a shared secret K and the current time; 'the verifier MUST NOT accept the second attempt of the OTP' (single use); at most one time step of network delay recommended.

NIST SP 800-63B (5.1.3.2 out-of-band verifiers): authentication invalid if not completed within 10 minutes; a secret is accepted only once during its validity period; rate-limiting required when the secret has under 64 bits of entropy (a six digit code is about 20 bits, my arithmetic: 10^6 = about 2^20).

Example numbers: the times 4:59 and 5:01, the code 482913 and 12:00:00 / 12:05:00 and '5 tries' are made-up illustrations. 'Five minutes' is a common choice, not a standard (NIST's cap is ten). 'Most systems store a deadline and compare on use' is a general-practice claim, not from a cited page; the Redis internals (absolute timestamp, lazy and active expiry) were not confirmed from the docs page.

lines.text: Your login code works at four fifty nine and fails at five oh one, so what is counting?
lines.caps: WORKS AT *4:59 | FAILS AT *5:01 | WHAT IS *COUNTING?

lines.text: The server saves the code with a deadline, the current time plus five minutes.
lines.caps: THE SERVER *SAVES IT | WITH A *DEADLINE | NOW PLUS *FIVE MINUTES

lines.text: When you type it, it compares the time now with that deadline, and rejects the code if it has passed.
Or the database does it: set a time to live, and the code simply disappears.
lines.caps: OR THE *DATABASE DOES IT | A TIME TO *LIVE | THE CODE *DISAPPEARS

lines.text: Authenticator apps skip storage: the code comes from a shared secret and the clock, and changes every thirty seconds.
lines.caps: APPS SKIP *STORAGE | A SHARED *SECRET + THE CLOCK | EVERY *THIRTY SECONDS

lines.text: But here's the catch: five minutes allows guessing, so a six digit code needs attempt limits and single use.
lines.caps: BUT THERE IS A *CATCH | FIVE MINUTES ALLOWS *GUESSING | ATTEMPT *LIMITS | *SINGLE USE

lines.text: So limit attempts, delete used codes, and keep it short; NIST caps it at ten minutes.
In most systems, expiry is just a stored deadline checked on use, not a timer running for every code.
lines.caps: A STORED *DEADLINE | CHECKED ON *USE | NOT A *TIMER
